title: How Organized Communities Are Rebuilding in the Wake of Venezuela’s Twin Earthquakes
author: Celina della Croce
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/ceclila1-680x453.jpeg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/09/11/how-
organized-communities-are-rebuilding-in-the-wake-of-venezuelas-twin-
earthquakes/)

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/ceclila1-680x453.jpeg)

The search for survivors in La Guaira in the days following the twin
earthquakes. Photo credit: [Rome Arrieche](http://@romearrie).

At 3:55 a.m. on June 25, a flicker of cellular service allowed Carlos to send
word to the outside world from the rubble of his home in La Guaira that he and
his family had survived the [twin
earthquakes](https://portal.globetrotter.media/es/2026/06/30/terremoto-en-
venezuela-la-lucha-por-sobrevivir/) that shook Venezuela’s capital region
hours earlier. “For now, I’m in a makeshift shelter near where my house used
to be,” he wrote. “We’re trying to help and rescue our neighbors.” Then the
service went out again.

In the days that followed, Carlos, his neighbors, state workers, and thousands
of Venezuelans [dug](https://thetricontinental.org/red-alert-22-venezuela/)
through rubble and what remained of their homes to pull out their family,
friends, and neighbors – both those who survived, and those who did not (6,462
and 6,509 respectively, according to latest official
[figures](https://www.independentespanol.com/noticias/america-
latina/aumenta-a-6-509-la-cifra-de-fallecidos-por-los-dos-terremotos-
del-24-de-junio-en-venezuela-b3038571.html)). Thousands more sought refuge
where they could, with the largest shelter, Caribbean Maritime University,
reporting an estimated 4,000 or more people in the early days (down to
[2,600](https://mazo4f.com/centro-de-recepcion-de-personas-afectadas-por-el-
doble-sismo-de-la-universidad-maritima-del-caribe-atiende-a-2600-venezolanos)
within a week as other shelters were set up to provide more dignified
conditions or as survivors found other housing solutions, and 830 as of late
August).

“It was severely overpopulated, with families sleeping in the hallways and
anywhere they could fit, but we couldn’t close the door to anyone who needed
help,” Carlos, who is currently the director of the Narciso Gonell Temporary
Shelter as well as a member of the Communard Union and the director of
security for the Ministry of Communes, told me.

Many of the officials in La Guaira tasked with this responsibility had also
been killed by the earthquakes – including
[half](https://www.elnacional.com/2026/07/gobernador-de-la-guaira-la-mitad-de-
los-directores-de-la-gobernacion-fallecieron-en-los-terremotos/) of the
directors in the governors’ office – adding yet another layer of challenge to
rescue and recovery efforts. “Despite the fact that the regional government
lost a significant part of its cabinet, those who took on this work were on
the ground doing what had to be done,” Juan, a state worker at the Narciso
Gonell Temporary Shelter, told me. Furthermore, he explained, “forty-nine
communal councils [organized neighborhoods] completely disappeared,” and with
them cadre who had been trained by years of the revolution. Nonetheless, the
existing organization built over the more than [two
decades](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/05/18/communal-consults-and-
venezuelas-fight-for-the-future/) of the Bolivarian Revolution made a
significant impact on the efficacy of rescue and relief efforts. Juan
explained that in less organized buildings – disproportionately the more
luxurious, privately built ones – rescue efforts were more difficult. “People
there didn’t know their neighbors. It’s not like that in the communes, where
everyone knows their neighbor and where they live.”

Despite tremendous losses, within days of the earthquakes, a combination of
state support, grassroots organizing structures, and the social fabric built
during the revolution created more shelters, services, and support systems for
the tens of thousands of survivors left unhoused, or _protegidos_(the
protected), as they are referred to in the government’s _campamentos
transitorios_ (temporary shelters). By 17 July,
[107](https://prensapresidencialvenezuela.gob.ve/index.php/2026/07/17/nuevo-
balance-oficial-reporta-21-mil-235-personas-ubicadas-en-campamentos-
transitorios/) shelters were created that housed 21,235 protegidos (with a
capacity for [25,282](https://mippci.gob.ve/balance-oficial-
reporto-107-campamentos-transitorios-atienden-a-mas-de-21-mil-personas-en-el-
pais/)), many of which are schools.

This terminology reflects a foundational priority in Venezuela’s temporary
shelters, which must not only provide housing, food, and adequate sanitary
conditions, but also a sense of normalcy, care, and dignity. Every meal is
planned with nutritionists, with Sundays featuring a special family meal and
activities. Psychologists come to the shelters two to three times a week and
offer individual counseling. A daily and weekly schedule features activities
for protegidos, especially for children. Common agreements outline quiet
hours, prohibit the consumption of alcohol, and enforce a zero-tolerance
policy for gender-based violence. Regular inventory is taken of the supplies
needed for protegidos, which is reported upwards and then restocked. Defined
roles outline who is responsible for each of the tasks required to maintain a
clean, safe, and caring environment, with many of the protegidos signing up as
volunteers to assist in tasks from cooking and cleaning to reconstruction and
renovation work in the shelters.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/cdc2-680x907.jpeg)

A child at the Maritime University shelter practices soccer ahead of the big
match. Photo: Celina della Croce.

**The Narciso Gonell Temporary Shelter**

“When we arrived [in the Narciso Gonell school] on 30 June,” Juan told me, “we
faced the huge challenge of adapting the infrastructure because it wasn’t
suitable for people to live here for as long as it takes for them to be
allocated their homes.” The high school lacked showers, mattresses, bunk beds,
air conditioning, and other key infrastructure needed to provide temporary
housing. It had also sustained damage during the earthquake, with cracks in
the basketball court making it unsafe for children to play.

At the same time, the often well-intentioned but insufficiently organized
drive to help was taking its toll. “People wanted to come and cheer up the
children, but all of the sudden you had a kid who had eaten twenty lollipops
running around on a sugar high until 3am. Despite good intentions, it was
contributing to an overall state of anxiety,” Carlos explained. Within hours,
however, the organizational structures built through the Bolivarian Revolution
were put to use. Juan recounted how Franklin, a member of the Hugo Chávez
Commune in La Guaira and a protegido at the Narciso Gonell shelter, was “among
those who convinced people… to move from their tents to Maritime University
[shelter] and then here [Narciso Gonell].” When some chose to remain in their
tents, communards, protegidos, and state officials brought them water and
other supplies. “All of those impacted collaborate here, organizing alongside
the institutions” Franklin told me.

“The people in this shelter have taught us a lesson,” Juan continued. “And the
lesson is that, when we’re organized – just as they are organized in their
communes and communal councils – everything runs more smoothly; everything is
easier.” Meanwhile, Carlos explained how unorganized volunteers ended up “re-
victimizing people who had already been victims of the earthquake. They
offered to donate but only if they could go up to [a protegido’s] room and
physically hand the person an arepa, or a tamal, or clothing… But imagine, if
ten people come to me, and there are ten people walking around their room…”

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/3.jpeg)

A caravan of motorcycles brings aid to La Guaira in the days following the
earthquake. Photo: [Rome Arrieche](http://@romearrie).

By the time I visited the Narciso Gonell Temporary Shelter in late August, the
basketball court had been repaired and repainted; 80 of the 265 protegidos had
signed up for scheduled volunteer tasks, with others stepping in to help
regularly; children were given a nutritious daily _merienda_ (snack) planned
alongside the Ministry of Nutrition in lieu of dozens of lollipops, and
solidarity brigades from across the country had arrived to meet the needs in
the shelters, with state officials, communards, protegidos, and volunteers
[working](https://www.comunas.gob.ve/2026/07/21/poder-popular-transforma-
campamento-transitorio-narciso-gonell-catia-la-mar/) hand in hand. As part of
a commitment by the Partido Socialista Unido de Venezuela (PSUV) to send
brigades from every state in the country to help with the shelters, plumbers,
civil engineers, and other specialists from Sucre state came to adapt and
improve the space, working alongside communes, volunteers, and the Ministry of
Public Works. They converted storage rooms into bathrooms with individual
shower stalls; built a laundry room; expanded and improved the potable water
system; installed air conditioners and a generator; weatherized windows;
repaired and painted the walls and basketball court; expanded the kitchen; and
more. Rooms that had two electrical outlets – sufficient to meet the classroom
needs – were fitted with ten outlets to meet the needs of the families
temporarily housed there and organized into demarcated sections for each
family with new mattresses, bunk beds, and a closet. Once school is back in
session in mid-September, that means that students will also benefit in the
long-term from the improved infrastructure.

Other brigades from across the country brought doctors and nurses (many
trained in Cuba), including specialists in pediatric and obstetric-
gynecological care, as well as supplies of fresh fruits, vegetables, and meat
donated to Narciso Gonell and other shelters by 72 communes across the
country. Yet others brought rescue workers who came to assist in the search
first for survivors and later for the dead. Others offered a variety of
cultural activities, from live concerts to juggling acts. Brigade members work
alongside protegidos, who themselves come from a range of professions: “we
have everything here – hairdressers, firefighters, teachers, bricklayers…”
Carlos told me. Each of these skills, alongside the needs and characteristics
of each protegido, has been carefully recorded by the shelters’ coordinators,
information that is both employed in the organization of the space as well as
to report needs to relevant institutions Sandra, a single mother of three and
who worked as a cook before the earthquakes, was one of those prioritized in
the state-funded entrepreneurship program Emprender Juntos, which gives
microloans to families to get back on their feet – “families that a bank would
never give a loan to,” Carlos said. “[Sandra] used to get into fights with
everyone,” a roommate confessed, but “she has completely changed. Now she’s
all smiles.”

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/4.jpeg)

A nurse and member of El Maizal Commune in Lara State describes the healthcare
system at the Narciso Gonell shelter, where she attends protegidos. Photo:
Celina della Croce.

**Humanitarian Aid and the Dispute for Dignity**

“This is like our second family,” Amelia, a protegida and pre-school teacher,
told me outside of the classroom-turned-beauty parlor in the Narciso Gonell
shelter. “We hope that soon we’ll have our own dignified homes,” Carlos added,
aware of the state of constant anxiety brought on by the uncertainty of the
when, the where, and the how as the state builds a
[plan](https://eldiario.com/2026/07/28/delcy-rodriguez-plan-creditos-
subsidios-viviendas-terremotos-venezuela/) to provide housing for the tens of
thousands of displaced, especially with schools set to
[reopen](https://www.mppe.gob.ve/media/filer_public/51/30/5130f43c-2857-458f-a99f-0236692c1156/calendario_escolar_meducacion_2026-2027.pdf)
on September 14. “But we hope that we’ll get to be neighbors.” In the midst of
massive loss and trauma, “this has been a gift from God,” Sandra’s roommate
added.

Yet this “gift” has not been without its disputes. In the midst of the chaos,
with 10,000 to 100,000 projected dead according to [early
estimates](https://es-us.noticias.yahoo.com/el-servicio-geologico-de-estados-
unidos-estima-entre-10000-y-100000-muertos-en-venezuela-065826599.html) from
the United States Geological Survey (USGS), NGOs, religious groups, and
foreign government agencies from across the world flooded the country. “We
gladly accept the materials and donations,” Carlos told me, but not at the
expense of dignity and respect. “It’s not profitable to overcome the crisis,”
he explained. “There is a territorial dispute: [many organizations] came with
resources but refused to recognize our systems of organization. As we
organized within our communes and the structures we’ve built, they told us no
– we’re the ones in charge. They want to disarticulate the social fabric we’ve
built.”

Furthermore, the practices of most NGOs clashed deeply with survivors and
their families – notably with the uncompromising expectation of dignity and
respect that has been woven into the fabric of Venezuelan society over the
more than two decades of the revolution. For instance, in contrast with the
regular psychological treatment offered at the shelters, reports proliferated
of NGOs handing out anti-anxiety medicine like candy without adequately
explaining to survivors what they were being given. You can’t sleep? Here,
take this, they were told. Others reported that some non-profits arrived with
lists of adoptive families, hoping to take children out of the country at a
moment when entire households had been killed and extended families had not
yet been able to determine who had survived or where they were.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/5.jpeg)

Rescue efforts in La Guaira in the days following the earthquakes. Photo:
[Rome Arrieche](http://@romearrie).

While over twenty thousand earthquake survivors have sought refuge in the
state’s temporary shelters, with the help of organized communities and
volunteers like Francisco, there is also “a dispute for the people,” Juan
Carlos, a member of the Communard Union, told me. As part of this dispute, a
variety of religious organizations (especially evangelical churches), NGOs,
and U.S. and other international agencies with varying motives have used the
havoc wreaked by the twin earthquakes to attempt to “to dismantle popular
organization.”

This is especially the case where concentrated clusters of informal tents have
sprung up in affected areas such as Mar Abajo, La Guaira. Here, a sea of
plastic tarps and tents stretch along the coastline bearing the names of
organizations like Samaritan’s Purse, U.S. Agency for International
Development (USAID), and United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) alongside
canopies set up to distribute bags of food and a government canteen that
provides three meals a day to 1,200 earthquake survivors. (It is worth noting
that USAID, whose logo can be seen across the tent settlements, has a long
[history](https://www.counterpunch.org/2014/04/25/the-dirty-hand-of-the-
national-endowment-for-democracy-in-venezuela/) of intervention in Venezuela.)

In addition to the services provided by the government and communes, there is
a “random handout” of aid, Justo, a leader of the Gran Cacique Mare Commune,
explained. “There are some people [receiving aid] who aren’t even from here,”
he continued. “They come from another area and want to get their hands on
benefits. Sometimes they come at night and set up camp around here to see
what’s being handed out to take away. Then they take their loot back there.
It’s tough… When charities arrive that operate outside of our system of
organization and lists, it’s a disaster.”

Justo, another member of the Gran Cacique Mare Commune and a protegido at the
Mar Abajo Baseball Field Temporary Shelter, explained that his commune is made
up of seven smaller communal councils, each with spokespeople and an
organizational system. Through this system, he said, the commune seeks to
“ensure that benefits are made collective and distributed to the whole
community.” Domingo chimed in: “when the first aid arrived, there was nothing…
Seeing that so many organizations were coming here, we quickly made a map of
each sector.” He pointed to the color-coded map, which identifies the level of
damage to each of the 1,616 homes in his commune as assessed by the
presidential committee (red for ‘high risk’ or uninhabitable, yellow for
restricted access, and green for homes deemed habitable) as well as the
demographic breakdown: the age of each survivor, how many families remain, how
many are living in tents or shelters, and the leaders in each of the seven
communal councils. “We’re not totally organized yet,” Justo said. But, Domingo
added, “we’re rebuilding our map of dreams.”

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/6.jpeg)

Alfredo, age thirteen, sorts and cleans tomatoes during summer vacation with
other members of the Sectores Unidos Commune in Villanueva, Lara, to get ready
for the market. His commune donated more than 3,000 kilos of the tomatoes,
bananas, and avocados that they produce, to Luis Hurtado Higuera and Narciso
Gonell Temporary shelters. Photo: Celina della Croce.

**The Media, Economic Sabotage, and the Opportunity of Disaster**

In this map are 720 “red” buildings – nearly half of the homes in the Gran
Cacique Mare Commune in Mar Abajo, La Guaira – including Justo’s home. Justo
explained that the extent of damage was due not only to the tremendous impact
of the back-to-back 7.2 and 7.5 earthquakes, but also to the deterioration
caused by a decade of the U.S.-led blockade. For instance, he explained, “ten
years of the [blockade](https://mronline.org/2023/08/18/how-u-s-sanctions-are-
a-tool-of-war-the-case-of-venezuela/) meant that people couldn’t afford to
invest in their homes, which affected many households. Our eternal enemy, the
salt air (_salitre_), also had a huge impact on housing; it’s terribly
corrosive. All of these factors compounded the impact of the twin
earthquakes.”

The U.S.-led blockade includes [more than
1,000](https://observatorio.gob.ve/#numeros-bloqueo-ingles-xpag-1/1/)
sanctions and unilateral coercive measures on Venezuela as well as forms of
unconventional, or
[hybrid](https://thetricontinental.org/dossier-36-twilight/), war, which
[seek](https://mronline.org/2023/08/18/how-u-s-sanctions-are-a-tool-of-war-
the-case-of-venezuela/) to pin the blame for widespread suffering on the
Venezuelan government and thereby push the population to
[overthrow](https://thetricontinental.org/newsletterissue/twelve-step-method-
to-conduct-regime-change-the-fifth-newsletter/) it without putting [boots on
the ground](https://www.commondreams.org/views/2019/06/16/why-venezuela-
vietnam-our-time). To report on the damage wrought by the twin earthquakes
while ignoring the [systematic
weakening](https://www.ohchr.org/en/documents/country-
reports/ahrc4859add2-visit-bolivarian-republic-venezuela-report-special) of
infrastructure and organization caused by the blockade – the very
infrastructure and organization needed to save lives – is, at best, to [lie by
omission](https://thetricontinental.org/red-alert-22-venezuela/).

Another form of this unconventional war against Venezuela is an ongoing [media
campaign](https://thetricontinental.org/red-alert-22-venezuela/), which
largely reported that the government was responsible for the extent of the
devastation caused by the earthquakes, due, for instance, to allegedly poorly
built public structures. However, within days it was reported that 80% of the
collapsed structures were
[built](https://portal.globetrotter.media/es/2026/06/30/terremoto-en-
venezuela-la-lucha-por-sobrevivir/) by the private sector – the very sector
that was strengthened when U.S. sanctions blocked the government from the
international financial system. In other words, far from the image it presents
of a good samaritan seeking to help a people in need, the U.S. in fact
contributed to the devastation and death wrought by the earthquakes through
years of economic and hybrid warfare.

In the wake of the twin earthquakes, as survivors grieve the loss of their
loved ones, homes, and entire communities, videos proliferate of survivors
decrying poor conditions, painting a picture of an absent state leaving
victims to fend for themselves (not unlike the reality faced by Hurricane
Katrina survivors in 2005 in New Orleans, United States, where I volunteered
in reconstruction efforts as a high school student). Yet there are a number of
different reasons that families have chosen to live in tents rather than in
government shelters.

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/7.jpeg)

A family enjoys a cultural activity and food at the Maritime University
shelter's dining area. Photo: Celina della Croce.

In some cases, families whose homes are undergoing repair and will be, but are
not yet, inhabitable camp out nearby, knowing that they will move back in once
the repairs are done (with at least 1,400 buildings
[repaired](https://www.elnacional.com/2026/09/delcy-rodriguez-
entrego-440-viviendas-rehabilitadas-en-el-sector-ruperto-lugo-tras-los-sismos-
de-
junio/?fbclid=IwY2xjawUMQCRwZG9mBWV4dG4DYWVtAjEwAGJyaWQRMURBaUNRNWwwdGhSWlR2bzFzcnRjBmFwcF9pZBAyMjIwMzkxNzg4MjAwODkyAAEe_JHbrvZ4C5RrXLSczynYU5HeWj6U996Do8rJbxQU7NU7VYNlK4EuhDppw6s_aem_5UnrUgB88DU7yuMTAXnnpg)
by the state so far). Others do not want to leave their neighborhoods, with no
guarantee of which shelter they will be offered and, for those whose homes
collapsed completely or are beyond repair (especially in zones along the
faultline that may not be deemed safe for reconstruction), what return the
reconstruction plan will offer them.

Other families have chosen to stay near the ruins of their homes and continue
the search for the remains of their loved ones as the government continues to
sort and remove rubble (with over 600,000 tons, or 28.61%, of the rubble
[cleared](https://www.independentespanol.com/noticias/america-
latina/aumenta-a-6-509-la-cifra-de-fallecidos-por-los-dos-terremotos-
del-24-de-junio-en-venezuela-b3038571.html)). The daughter of Domingo’s
predecessor as the coordinator of the [_sala de
autogobierno_](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/05/18/communal-consults-and-
venezuelas-fight-for-the-future/) (self-governance room), Ruth, is among those
who continue to sift through the rubble in hopes of providing her mother with
a proper burial. “She was an incredible woman,” Domingo said. “It’s tragic.
[Her daughter] has been looking for her in the rubble day and night for more
than two months, but they haven’t been able to find her body… It’s like
finding a needle in a haystack amid so much rubble.”

However, there is also a segment of the population that has been drawn into
media and ideological warfare, vesting their hopes for the future in NGOs,
religious organizations, and the U.S. – the very government that has strangled
its economy, contributed to conditions that magnified the scale of the
disaster, and bombed La Guaira and Caracas earlier this year during the
abduction of President Nicolás Maduro and First Lady Cilia Flores. This is
only one sector of a much larger population of tens of thousands of survivors
who lost their homes, yet it is the only one reported with any frequency in
the media. As Justo told me, there is a sustained effort to “create false
perspectives and fake news… We have to find a way to dispel those myths.”

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/8.jpeg)

A member of Guardia del Pueblo (People’s Guards) serves as a wheelchair
attendant for a protegida at the Maritime University shelter on the outskirts
of the dancefloor. Photo: Celina della Croce.

Behind the media and ideological campaign unfolding in La Guaira lie deeper
geopolitical and economic interests. For one, Juan Carlos explained, La Guaira
is “the most important port in Venezuela. [It] is useful to the Americans for
economic reasons – for businesspeople who want to invest in tourism here,
[and] to control the port.” In order to do this, he continued, the role of
NGOs, religious organizations, and other foreign agencies is key in
“exercising ideological control and cultural domination… to break with the
communal fabric and social fabric” built over the years of the revolution.
With a foothold in communities deepened through humanitarian aid in a moment
of profound suffering and disaster, these organizations are better positioned
to spread an ideology to ensure that “there is no resistance to [foreign]
capital seeking to enter La Guaira.”

Furthermore, he pointed out, La Guaira is a key tourist destination thirty
minutes from the capital, Caracas; near an international airport; and home to
some of the country’s most beautiful beaches, surrounded by the Waraira Repano
National Park. “That is why the _gringos_ need people to be indoctrinated, to
be part of a cult, to believe in God – or even to believe that capital is God,
that it is on its way and that it will save the people.”

This is the scenario in which national and international media have entered
communities devastated by the twin earthquakes in search of discontent to
paint a severely biased picture of the reality on the ground, casting a blind
eye toward survivors like Domingo, Justo, and Juan. “This is important,” Justo
told me: “you’re here from the U.S., where they sell the image that Venezuela
is bad, it’s a disaster, that all you’ll see is the ruptured streets [from the
earthquakes]. But you have to come to Venezuela and see if that’s true. What
they do is sell problems, not solutions. So those of us who are here – and my
home was declared red – I’m not here just to be here. This is my home. I’m
looking for solutions.”

![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/9.jpeg)

A communal policewoman dances with a child at El Luis Hurtado Higuera shelter.
Photo: Celina della Croce.

**Building the Future**

Without dignity at its core, a meal may look like a can of tuna and saltine
crackers offered with pity or condescension, and shelter like plastic
stretched over dirt and rubble, but for people like Carlos, Justo, Domingo,
Francisco, and Juan, who have set out amid the rubble to rebuild their
communities with culture, care, and collective life woven into each aspect of
daily life, this is far from enough.

On a Sunday in late August, the temporary shelter at the Caribbean Maritime
University looked more like a fairground than a refugee camp. A brigade from
the state of Táchira led by Grecia Colmenares, a deputy to and the second vice
president of the National Assembly, had arrived to coordinate the week’s
cultural activities as part of an ongoing rotation, converting the open-air
canteen into a dancefloor surrounded by booths serving ice cream, Andean soup,
and the best sweets and _pastelitos_ of their region. Members of the _Guardia
del Pueblo_(People’s Guards), a sector of Venezuela’s armed forces, served as
wheelchair attendants and peacekeepers, breaking up the occasional fight
between children over who received which doll, or whether or not a goal during
a soccer match had been fairly called. In the tent in which the Gran Cacique
Mare Commune’s self-governance room is currently operating at the Mar Abajo
Baseball Field temporary shelter, Domingo and Justo rebuild not only their
community but their dreams for the future and how to lift up the communities
around them. Wendy, a protegida and young mother at the Narciso Gonell
shelter, enjoyed a child-free moment during breakfast as she watches her
neighbors take turns fawning over her eleven-month-old daughter and three-
year-old son. At the Luis Hurtado Higuera shelter in El Junquito, a communal
policewoman danced with a child to the sounds of an Afro-Caribbean percussion
group from the [_Ruta de la
Esperanza_](https://www.mincultura.gob.ve/mincultura-activa-la-ruta-de-la-
esperanza-para-brindar-acompanamiento-emocional-a-la-infancia-ante-
emergencia/) (Route of Hope).

After the concert at the Luis Hurtado Higuera shelter came to a close, two
teenage boys swept the common area. I asked why they had volunteered to clean
up. One of them snickered, his eyes reflecting the universal teenage “duh…”
that transcends any spoken language. _Because it’s dirty_ , he said. I pressed
further. _Because that’s what we do. That’s what it is to be Venezuelan_ , his
friend chimed in _._ To take care of each other. To build hope amid the
rubble. To [build](https://thetricontinental.org/dossier-the-future/) the
world we deserve to live in and the [new human
